Senses.PreferredTarget: the formal end of a seasonal monastic restriction
SearchAliases: release day after the restriction period
Senses.Explanation: The formal release that ends a monastery's bounded seasonal restriction and allows monks to disperse. An impersonal narrator labels Zhengfa Ximing's following hall address as delivered at release, while Jie Weizhou and Miyun Yuanwu date the event and three reviewed unnamed monks make it the subject of public questions to Feiyin Tongrong, Huayan Shengke, and Chaozong Tongren. The compound occurs 1,683 times in 241 allowlisted texts; 153 occurrences in 43 texts label a hall address at release, and nine in seven label a small gathering. Jie Weizhou calls the fifteenth day of the first month the winter release after the restriction began on the fifteenth day of the tenth month. Miyun Yuanwu names the fifteenth day of the seventh month as release after an opening on the fifteenth day of the fourth month, and elsewhere says on release day that the brothers go east and west (兄弟東去西去, “the brothers go east and west”). In the three public questions, an unnamed monk asks Feiyin for a release-period saying and Feiyin answers “the monastery gate is wide open” (山門八字開); another unnamed monk asks Huayan for a release sentence and Huayan answers “tighten your sandals” (緊俏草鞋); a third unnamed monk asks Chaozong how he releases the restriction after quoting a rope tightening in water.
Senses.Note: This primary sense is the dated communal event. The headword occurs in 28 direct binding/release pairings across 22 texts, 23 exact “release day” strings in 16 texts, and 50 exact “today release” strings in 36 texts. Lianyue Guangsi, Huayan Huanchu, and Konggu Daocheng explicitly use the same compound for a different event—an individual's release when an inward obstruction breaks—so their definitions remain sense 2 rather than being folded into this calendar sense.

Senses.PreferredTarget: an individual's release when an inward obstruction breaks
AlternateTargets: personal release from an inward restriction
the breaking of a self-bound restriction
Senses.Explanation: A personal release in which something restricting the person breaks apart. Lianyue Guangsi, Huayan Huanchu, and Konggu Daocheng explicitly borrow the institutional term for this different event rather than merely offering readings of the calendar release, while Shiyu Mingfang supplies its negative boundary. Lianyue says that binding comes from one's own mind and release comes from one's own mind (結制從自心結，解制從自心解, “the restriction is bound from one's own mind; the restriction is released from one's own mind”); he then calls the chest's obstructing thing dissolving like ice and broken tiles “release from the restriction” (胸中礙膺之物瓦解冰消，謂之解制). Huayan says that after the sky-covering net is broken and one emerges beyond the three realms, this is called release (忽然打破漫天網子，㘞地一聲，超出三界，名為解制也). Konggu pairs the beginning of entry with binding and calls the moment when accumulated obstructions dissolve like ice and broken tiles at awakening's end “release” (一刻冰消瓦解，悟道之終名為解制). Shiyu says that mistaking raised fists, pointing fingers, wild speech, and shouts for marvelous functioning does not deserve the name release (不唯不得名為解制).
Senses.Note: This sense is split because Lianyue Guangsi, Huayan Huanchu, and Konggu Daocheng explicitly use the same word for a different event: not the monastery's dated permission to disperse, but a claimed change in an individual described through self-binding, an obstructing thing dissolving, or an enclosing net breaking. The entry reports only their attested predicates and adds no outside system or prescribed procedure.
